# Rental property condition reports

Official information by:NSW Fair Trading

Housing and construction

[Listen](https://app-oc.readspeaker.com/cgi-bin/rsent?customerid=11246&lang=en_au&readclass=dcs-readspeaker-target%2crs_read&url=https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports "Listen to this page using ReadSpeaker webReader")

* * *

The condition report is evidence of how a rental property was before a tenant moved in. It is filled in at the beginning and end of a tenancy.

On this page

*   [Moving in](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports#toc-moving-in)
*   [Moving out](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports#toc-moving-out)
*   [Sample condition report](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports#toc-sample-condition-report)
*   [Legislation supporting this page](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports#toc-legislation-supporting-this-page)
*   [Related rules and guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/rental-property-condition-reports#toc-related-rules-and-guidance)

### Key information

*   A condition report records the general condition of the property, room by room, including fixtures and fittings. It is evidence of how the property was before the tenant moved in.
*   At the end of a tenancy, the condition report can be used to check [what is fair wear and tear](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties") over the time of the tenancy and what might be damage that the tenant needs to fix before they can finalise their tenancy.
*   The more detail, including time-stamped photographs, in a condition report, the less likely disputes will arise at the end of a tenancy.
*   All damage, including minor damage, should be noted and described on the report
*   Any visible hazards relating to electricity (e.g. a loose or damaged electricity outlet socket, loose wiring or sparking power points) should be noted
*   Faulty electricity sockets or loose wiring may be deemed as an[urgent repair](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/urgent-repairs-residential-rental-properties "Urgent repairs in residential rental properties").

*   Information on whether[smoke alarms](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/smoke-alarms-a-rental-property "Smoke alarms in a rental property")are installed (as required by legislation) and the dates that they were last checked and had battery replacement needs to be included
*   Tenants and landlords need to confirm if there are any safety switches and if they are working, which can only be done if the agent or landlord and tenant has done a test
*   The Tribunal can make orders about either amending or not amending a condition report as they see fit.

## Moving in

### Landlord's responsibilities

A landlord or agent must:

*   fill out a condition report before a tenant moves in
*   give two paper copies, or one electronic copy, to the tenant either before or at the time the tenancy agreement is given to the tenant to sign.

### Tenant's responsibilities

Tenants should:

*   complete their part of the condition report
*   take photos to go with the condition report - making sure to include time stamps to show when images were taken
*   return one completed copy to the landlord or agent within seven days of[moving in](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/starting-a-residential-tenancy/signing-a-lease-and-moving "Signing a lease and moving in")
*   keep the other copy for their records.

Note that:

*   a new condition report is not needed if the same people renew the tenancy agreement, or if a new co-tenant or occupant moves in.

## Moving out

A tenant and the landlord or agent should each have a copy of the condition report they filled in at the beginning of the tenancy.

[When a tenant moves out](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/ending-a-residential-tenancy/moving-out-of-a-rental-home "Moving out of a rental property"), they will need to fill the condition report in again. This should be done by the landlord or agent and tenant in each other's presence.However, it can be done without the other person being present provided they have been given a reasonable opportunity to be present.

The report should be filled out with as much detail and accuracy as possible.

If there is a[disagreement or dispute](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/resolving-residential-tenancy-disputes "Resolving residential tenancy disputes")about missing items or damage, the condition report can be used as evidence.

## Sample condition report

[Download a sample residential tenancy condition report](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/residential-tenancy-condition-report "Residential tenancy condition report").

### Get help from NSW Fair Trading

Ask a question, get support, make a complaint, give feedback or get help with a dispute on matters relating to residential tenancies.

NSW Fair Trading call centre: [13 32 20](tel:133220)

Monday to Friday, 8:30am-5pm

*   [Make a tenancy or other real estate related enquiry at NSW Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/departments-and-agencies/fair-trading/complaints-and-enquiries) 
*   [Provide feedback or make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints") 
*   [Get information and advice about dealing with tenancy disputes](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/resolving-residential-tenancy-disputes "Resolving residential tenancy disputes") 

## Legislation supporting this page

*   [Condition reports, Section 29, Residential Tenancies Act 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.29)
*   [Condition report evidence of condition of premises, Section 30, Residential Tenancies Act 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.30)
*   [Remedies for disputes about condition reports, Section 31, Residential Tenancies Act 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.31)

title: Sharing a residential rental property
text:
## Key information

*   There are 3 key ways to share a rental property. Each has different requirements for tenants.
*   A tenant must get a landlord’s written permission to sub-let or transfer any part of the property.
*   A landlord cannot unreasonably say no to requests to sub-let part of the property or to add one or more co-tenants to the tenancy.
*   The only costs a landlord or agent can charge for a sub-let or co-tenancy are the landlord's reasonable costs of giving consent.
*   Co-tenants can share and manage rental bonds using Rental Bonds Online through the principal tenant.
*   There is a form to update the bond records if there are any shared tenancy changes.
*   Each tenant’s bond contribution needs to be recorded on the Tenancy Agreement when it is completed.

There are 3 key sharing arrangements for a rental property. Each arrangement has different requirements.

### Sub-letting

In a sub-letting arrangement, the tenant can rent part or all the property to another person. In this arrangement the tenant who subleases to another tenant or tenants (known as the ‘head tenant’) has the same legal responsibilities towards their subtenant as a landlord. The head tenant remains the landlord's tenant and is still responsible for the tenancy, including the actions of the sub-tenant.

### Transferring or assigning the agreement

If a tenant transfers or assigns the tenancy agreement, they are inviting someone to be added to or take over the agreement. The existing agreement transfers to the new tenant or co-tenant. This includes any remaining fixed term period and the rent payable. There is no need to sign a new agreement, but it is best to put the arrangement in writing to avoid any disputes later.

### Additional occupants

An additional occupancy arrangement is when a tenant informally invites someone to stay with them. This could be a family member, friend or stranger and it may be a temporary or permanent arrangement.

## Consent from the landlord

A tenant must get a landlord’s written permission to sub-let or transfer any part of the property.

If a tenant does this without consent, they are breaching the terms of the tenancy agreement.

Having an 'additional occupant' does not need permission, but a tenant must not exceed the maximum number of permitted occupants stated on the tenancy agreement.

In a social housing arrangement, the social housing provider's own policies and procedures apply.

## When can a landlord say no?

A landlord cannot say no unreasonably to requests to sub-let part of the property or to add one or more co-tenants to the tenancy.

Examples of when it is reasonable for a landlord to say no include, but are not limited to, if:

*   the total number of occupants permitted under the agreement would be exceeded
*   the total number of occupants would exceed any local council rules and regulations
*   the person being proposed is listed on a tenancy database
*   they reasonably believe it would result in the property being overcrowded.

If a tenant’s request is refused, and they believe the decision is unreasonable, they can apply to the Tribunal to hear their case.

A landlord can refuse consent to a request to sub-let the whole property or transfer the whole tenancy, regardless of whether the refusal is reasonable.

## Managing the rental bond online in a subletting arrangement

The head tenant must:

*   [register with Rental Bonds Online](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants")
*   invite the tenant to use the online rental bond service, and give the tenant a reasonable opportunity to use the service to deposit the bond with Fair Trading or decline the invitation
*   not ask for more than 4 weeks’ rent as a bond
*   lodge the bond with NSW Fair Trading within 10 days of receipt. The head tenant must not keep the bond amount in their own bank account.

Any party to the sub-tenancy agreement may make a claim to Fair Trading for payment of the bond paid under the agreement.

## Costs to tenants

A landlord or agent cannot charge a tenant for a sub-let or co-tenancy, other than for the landlord's reasonable expenses of giving consent.

A landlord can only charge a tenant for a reasonable expense that the landlord has paid for.

If more than one tenant is on the bond (2 or more co-tenants), for Rental Bonds Online, the tenants must decide who will be the 'principal tenant'.

The principal tenant acts on behalf of all tenants. They must:

*   [register with Rental Bonds Online](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-rental-bonds/rental-bonds-online-for-tenants "Rental Bonds Online for tenants") and pay the bond money to NSW Fair Trading
*   provide all co-tenants' contact details to keep them informed of any changes to the bond
*   at the end of the tenancy, respond to or submit a claim for refund of bond money on behalf of all the tenants
*   distribute any bond refund to the other tenants.

The other tenants may view details and receive copies of notifications sent to the principal tenant, but they cannot log on to Rental Bonds Online or do any bond transactions.

The principal tenant may log on to Rental Bonds Online at any time. They can do this to:

*   view the status of the bond
*   view any notifications
*   create or respond to transactions that a landlord or agent makes
*   update their co-tenants' contact details
*   change other details, including the bank account that a refund will be made to
*   submit a refund claim at the end of the tenancy.

A principal tenant can reuse their Rental Bonds Online account to pay their bond for any future property they may rent, if the managing agent or landlord is registered to use the service.

The landlord or the tenant usually ends a tenancy by giving notice to the other party. The tenant vacates the property by the date specified in the termination notice. Minimum notice periods will apply for different tenancy agreements or reasons to end a tenancy. There may also be [break fees or other costs if a tenancy is ended early](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/breaking-a-fixed-term-residential-tenancy-early "Breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy early").

It is important to tell NSW Fair Trading of any changes to co-tenants for a shared tenancy with a residential online or paper bond by completing and lodging a change of shared tenancy request form.

[Download the change of shared tenancy request form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/change-of-shared-tenancy-arrangement-form "Change of shared tenancy arrangement form").

### Co-tenant moving out

If a co-tenant moves out of a shared tenancy and requests their share of the bond, the remaining tenant/s must pay it back – less any rent owed to them by the co-tenant or other reasonable costs relating to the rented property – within 14 days of the request.

This does not apply if the former co-tenant:

*   has debts that exceed the amount of bond money they paid
*   has been excluded from the premises by a final apprehended violence order.

If the remaining co-tenant/s do not repay the former co-tenant's share of the bond within 14 days, the former co-tenant may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring payment of the amount owed. The application must be made within 6 months after the day the tenancy ends.

### Change of principal tenant

*   If the principal tenant is changing, the remaining co-tenants need to nominate a new principal tenant.
*   The agent or landlord needs to send the new principal tenant a link to accept the role.

When the new principal tenant is in place, a change of shared tenancy arrangement form should be completed and signed by all parties.

A claim can only be made on a bond once the tenancy agreement for that property has ended. This is the case even if a co-tenant moves out, but other tenants remain in the property under the tenancy agreement.

A co-tenant moving out of a shared tenancy can request their share of the bond from the other co-tenants (as per the process outlined above).

For shared tenancies (2 or more tenants on the bond), only the principal tenant with a Rental Bonds Online account can submit the claim on behalf of the other tenants.

The principal tenant who acts on behalf of all co-tenants for the shared rental should:

*   submit or respond to a claim for refund of bond money at the end of the tenancy
*   distribute the bond refund to the other tenants.

A tenant or former tenant may apply to the Tribunal for an order about the payment of a rental bond between co-tenants. Applications must be made within 6 months after the tenancy ends.

The Tribunal can decide how much of the bond each co-tenant should receive. In making its decision, the Tribunal may consider each co-tenant's original bond contribution. Any outstanding costs or charges may be deducted before the bond is paid.

To support this process, residential tenancy agreements signed after 21 September 2026 record each co-tenant’s original bond contribution.

[Log in to Rental Bonds Online](https://rbo.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/tenant/login)if you are the principal tenant and need to claim the bond.

[Learn more about getting your bond back](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-your-bond-back "Getting your bond back at the end of a tenancy")at the end of a tenancy, at the end of a tenancy, including how to claim back a paper bond.

A tenant can end their part of a shared tenancy immediacy, without penalty, if they or their dependent child are affected by domestic abuse.

For more information about ending a tenancy in circumstances of domestic abuse, please visit [Ending a tenancy because of domestic violence and abuse](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/ending-a-tenancy-because-of-domestic-violence-and-abuse "Ending a tenancy because of domestic violence and abuse").

If your part of a shared tenancy ends but other tenants stay in the property, you can ask them to repay your share of the rental bond.

If you do not feel safe or comfortable asking the remaining tenants for your share of the bond, or if there is a dispute, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order about how the bond should be paid between co-tenants.

Money cannot be deducted from your rental bond for damage caused by domestic abuse if you were not the perpetrator of the domestic abuse. For more information on getting your rental bond returned, please visit [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/tenant-protections-for-domestic-violence-and-abuse-a-rental-property "Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property").

# Off campus accommodation

Places to stay and tips to find housing near or outside the University

![Image 3](https://www.sydney.edu.au/content/dam/campus-facilities-and-amenities/accommodation/accomm.jpg)

Whether you're looking for a boarding house or a modern, purpose-built student apartment, there's plenty of accommodation options near the University of Sydney and across the city.

Enjoy convenient, comfortable living with easy access to campus and everything Sydney has to offer!

[](https://usyd.starrezhousing.com/StarRezPortalX/7C3CEFBB/1/1/Home-Welcome_to_the_Unive?UrlToken=308793FE)

Apply to live in Kensington through the Accommodation Portal

* * *

## Accommodation

Accommodation options located near campus including purpose-built student accommodation and apartments designed for comfort and convenience.

*   [Sydney University Village](https://www.mystudentvillage.com/au/sydney-university-village/)
*   [Iglu](http://www.iglu.com.au/)

*   [Belong premium apartments](https://www.belonghere.me/premium-secure-accommodation-for-university-of-sydney-students)

* * *

## Boarding houses

Common around the inner west of Sydney, offering a similar collegiate experience to living on campus. Most are run by a church or humanitarian group.

What’s included in your rent varies from one place to another.

### Your options

*   [Arundel House](http://www.arundelhouse.asn.au/)
*   [Flo Harris Lodge](http://www.floharrislodge.org.au/)
*   [St. Barnabas Terraces](http://www.terraces.com.au/)

* * *

## Rental tips

### Explore surrounding suburbs

Our campuses border some of Sydney's most colourful suburbs, such as Newtown, Redfern and Glebe near the Camperdown/Darlington campus, and Camden at the Camden campus.

Check for verified listings for these areas on common rental sites, such as:

*   [Domain](http://www.domain.com.au/home?mode=rent)
*   [Flatmates](https://flatmates.com.au/)
*   [Realestate](http://www.realestate.com.au/rent)

### Factor in other costs

In addition to rent, you'll need to cover:

*   Bills, such as gas, electricity and internet
*   Furniture, as many properties come unfurnished
*   Bond, which is normally equivalent to four weeks rent
*   Transportation, if your rental isn't near the University

### Apply early

Accommodation near or on campus is extremely popular and can fill up fast, especially at the start of the semester. Start looking at least 2–3 months before you want to move in. You need time to check a few places before making a decision.

### Inspect the property

**Check the place before you pay**

Thoroughly inspect any property before paying a deposit or signing a contract. Never pay money through a funds transfer to a private rental agency or individual you don’t know. One option to consider is short-term housing which can be arranged before you arrive, which gives you time to search for a longer-term option.

For more information about how to spot a scam and get help,visit [Scamwatch](https://www.scamwatch.gov.au/get-help/where-to-get-help).

**Ask the landlord or property manager questions**

Write a list of questions and ask the landlord or property manager. Does the rental include utilities or internet access? Are you allowed to have guests? What facilities are shared? What about pets, parking, bicycle lockup?

### Know your tenant rights

Check out these resources:

*   [Fair Trading NSW](https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-property/renting)
*   [Tenants NSW](http://www.tenants.org.au/)
*   [Residential Tenancies Act](https://www.tenants.org.au/factsheet-01-residential-tenancies-act)
*   [SRC's legal advice for undergraduate students](https://srcusyd.net.au/src-help/src-legal-service/)

title: Tenants and rent increases
text:
Rent increases during a tenancy and how to resolve disputes about rent increases.

* * *

On this page

*   [When and how often can rent be increased](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-increases#toc-when-and-how-often-can-rent-be-increased)
*   [How a rent increase happens](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-increases#toc-how-a-rent-increase-happens)
*   [Negotiating a rent increase](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-increases#toc-negotiating-a-rent-increase)
*   [Disputing a rent increase](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-increases#toc-disputing-a-rent-increase)
*   [Resources and tools](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-increases#toc-resources-and-tools)
*   [Related information](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-increases#toc-related-information)

## When and how often can rent be increased

*   Rent cannot be raised within the first 12 months of a tenancy.
*   After an increase, the landlord must wait at least 12 months before another increase.
*   Increases do not have to be written down in the agreement.
*   These rules apply to periodic agreements and fixed term agreements, except for fixed term agreements of less than 2-years that began before 13 December 2024.

For fixed term agreements of less than 2 years that began before 13 December 2024:

*   **where there is no rent increase amount or calculation method written in the agreement,** the rent cannot be increased. When the fixed term ends, these agreements will move to the standard rule that limits rent increases to once every 12 months, like all other tenancies.
*   **where the agreement has a written rent increase amount or calculation method,** the rent can only be increased by following what the written agreement says. The agreement must have the amount of the increase or the exact method of calculating the increase (e.g. a dollar amount or percentage). The increase is not valid if the calculation method is unclear, as the tenant must know exactly what they will need to pay. For example, ‘in line with the market’ or ‘by the rate of inflation’ are unclear and not valid. When the fixed term ends, these agreements will move to the standard rule that limits rent increases to once every 12 months, like all other tenancies.  

### Renewing or replacing your lease

When you renew your agreement or switch to a different type of lease, it’s still considered the same rental agreement for the purposes of rent increase rules if:

*   the landlord hasn’t changed
*   at least one of the tenants is the same, and
*   the tenant has not moved out of the property between agreements.

This means that if a tenant is already living in the property and the agreement is renewed or the lease type changes, the landlord must wait at least 12 months from the last increase before they can raise the rent.

### Social housing agreements and rent increases

Rent can be increased under a social housing tenancy agreement more than once in 12 months if the increases are only due to a tenant’s rent rebate.

For example, social housing agreements may be reviewed to check that the rent rebate offered is in line with the tenant’s income.

For more information on rent and subsidies for social housing, visit [**Understanding rent, subsidies and reviews**](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/social-affordable/public-housing-tenants/paying-rent-and-other-charges/rent-subsidies-and-reviews)[.](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/social-affordable/public-housing-tenants/paying-rent-and-other-charges/rent-subsidies-and-reviews "Understanding rent, subsidies and reviews")

## How a rent increase happens

A landlord or agent must provide a tenant with written notice of a rent increase 60 days or more before the increase will take effect.

The landlord can either write their own notice, send the tenant an email, or use our notice of rent increase form. The notice must:

*   state the proposed new amount of rent (not the amount of the increase)
*   state the date from which the increased rent is payable, and
*   be signed, dated and properly addressed to the tenant.

[Download our notice of rent increase form](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/notice-of-rent-increase "Notice of rent increase")

## Negotiating a rent increase

If you think a proposed rent increase is too high then, before the new rent amount starts, you can:

*   use the NSW Government's [Rent Check](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-check "Rent Check")tool to compare your proposed rent with the median rent range in your postcode
*   negotiate with the landlord to reduce the amount of the increase or to withdraw the increase altogether.

If the negotiation is successful, get the landlord or agent's agreement in writing.

If the landlord or agent agrees to a lower increase, it is not necessary for them to send another 60-day notice to you, and the new lower rent increase is due from the same date the original increase was payable.

To get help or make a complaint, you can [contact NSW Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "Residential tenancy complaints") or you can go to the[Tenants’ Union of NSW](https://www.tenants.org.au/ "Tenants' Union of New South Wales (https://www.tenants.org.au/)")for legal advice, assistance, and information to tenants.

## Disputing a rent increase

If you cannot reach an agreement with your agent or landlord, you:

*   can apply to the [NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)](https://www.ncat.nsw.gov.au/ncat/case-types/housing-and-property/tenancy.html "Apply for help resolving your dispute at NCAT (https://www.ncat.nsw.gov.au/ncat/case-types/housing-and-property/tenancy.html)") within 30 days of receiving the rent increase notice if you believe that the rent increase is excessive
*   will have to prove that the increase is excessive.

Some of the main evidence the Tribunal considers is comparable rents for similar properties in the same area, the state of repair and amenities provided in the property and the landlord’s expenses.

The Tribunal has the power to set the rent for the next 12 months.

Request advice before a Tribunal hearing

Do you have a date for a hearing in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)? Get advice from your local Tenants Advice and Advocacy Service.

[Use the Tenants' Union request form](https://www.tenants.org.au/ncatadvice)

## Resources and tools

### Rent Check

Rent Check allows renters, landlords and the community to quickly and easily check and compare the median rent range in any NSW postcode. Get started now.

[Learn more about Rent Check](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/rent-check "Rent Check")

![Image 1: A man and woman in a rental property looking at a laptop](https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/styles/_medium/public/2024-07/Rent%20Price%20Check%20Tool_0.jpeg?itok=ndjTFCE3)

*   [Resolving residential tenancy disputes](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/resolving-residential-tenancy-disputes)
*   [Residential tenancy complaints](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints)

title: Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties
text:
# Fair wear and tear versus damage in rental properties

Official information by:NSW Fair Trading

Housing and construction

[Listen](https://app-oc.readspeaker.com/cgi-bin/rsent?customerid=11246&lang=en_au&readclass=dcs-readspeaker-target%2crs_read&url=https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "Listen to this page using ReadSpeaker webReader")

* * *

What is 'fair wear and tear' and what is damage in a rental property? Find out what the differences are and who is responsible for repairs and maintenance.

On this page

*   [Tenants' responsibilities](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties#toc-tenants-responsibilities)
*   [Landlord or agent's responsibilities](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties#toc-landlord-or-agents-responsibilities)
*   [Examples](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties#toc-examples)
*   [Get help from NSW Fair Trading](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties#toc-get-help-from-nsw-fair-trading)
*   [Legislation supporting this page](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties#toc-legislation-supporting-this-page)
*   [Related rules and guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties#toc-related-rules-and-guidance)

## Tenants' responsibilities

At the end of a tenancy, the tenant is responsible for leaving the property as near as possible to the same condition as when they started living in it.

The tenant is responsible for negligent, irresponsible or intentional actions that cause damage to the property. They will need to[organise and pay for repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done "Getting repairs done on a rental property")for damage they have caused or allowed (for example, by other occupants or guests).

However, the tenant is not responsible for 'fair wear and tear'.

### Property damage caused by domestic abuse

A tenant is also not financially responsible for property damage caused by domestic abuse if they are not the perpetrator of the abuse.

This applies regardless of whether the damage was caused by a co-tenant, occupant, guest or another person. In these circumstances, the landlord or agent cannot deduct money from the tenant’s bond for damage caused by domestic abuse. For more information on property damage liability, please visit [Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property](https://Tenant protections for domestic violence and abuse in a rental property).

## Landlord or agent's responsibilities

Landlords and agents must provide a rental property that meets[minimum standards](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/minimum-standards-for-rental-properties "[Rule] Minimum standards for rental properties")and maintain the property to meet those standards. They are expected to[respond in reasonable time to requests for repairs](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done "Getting repairs done on a rental property")from tenants.

## Examples

See below for examples of fair wear and tear versus damage.

### Curtains

*   Fair wear and tear – faded curtains or frayed cords
*   Damage – missing or torn curtains

### Carpet

*   Fair wear and tear – furniture indentations and traffic marks on the carpet
*   Damage – stains or burn marks on the carpet

### Floors

*   Fair wear and tear – scuffed up wooden floors
*   Damage – badly scratched or gouged wooden floors

### Paint

*   Fair wear and tear – faded, chipped or cracked paint
*   Damage – unapproved, poor quality paint job

### Kitchen

*   Fair wear and tear – worn kitchen benchtop
*   Damage – burns or cuts in benchtop

### Doors and windows

*   Fair wear and tear – loose hinges or handles on doors or windows and worn sliding tracks
*   Damage – broken glass

### Water stains

*   Fair wear and tear – water stains on carpet from rain through leaking roof or bad plumbing
*   Damage – water stains on carpet caused by overflowing bath or indoor pot plants

### Walls

*   Fair wear and tear – paint worn off wall near light switch
*   Damage – damage to paint caused by removing posters stuck with blu-tack or sticky tape

## Get help from NSW Fair Trading

Ask a question, get support, make a complaint, give feedback or get help with a dispute on matters relating to residential tenancies.

NSW Fair Trading call centre: [**13 32 20**](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/fair-wear-and-tear-versus-damage-rental-properties "tel:133220")

Monday to Friday, 8:30am-5pm

*   [**Make a tenancy or other real estate related enquiry at NSW Fair Trading**](https://www.nsw.gov.au/departments-and-agencies/fair-trading/complaints-and-enquiries "https://www.nsw.gov.au/departments-and-agencies/fair-trading/complaints-and-enquiries")
*   [**Provide feedback or make a complaint to NSW Fair Trading**](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints "https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/residential-tenancy-complaints")
*   [**Get information and advice about dealing with tenancy disputes**](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/resolving-residential-tenancy-disputes "https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/resolving-residential-tenancy-disputes")

## Legislation supporting this page

*   [Use of premises by tenant, Section 51, Residential Tenancies Act 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.51)
*   [Limit on liability of tenant for actions of other tenants occurring during domestic violence offences, Section 54A, Residential Tenancies Act 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.54A)
*   [Matters that may be subject of rental bond claim, Section 166, Residential Tenancies Act, 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.166)
*   [Liability of tenant for actions of others, Section 54, Residential Tenancies Act 2010](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/2023-08-03/act-2010-042#sec.54)

title: Minimum notice periods for access to rental property
text:
Tenants have the right to reasonable peace, comfort and privacy when renting. However,there are times when a landlord, agent or authorised person can enter the property without the tenant’s consent even if the tenant is not home, provided that the[provided that a valid reason and required notice have been given](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/landlord-access-and-entry-to-a-rental-property "Landlord access and entry to a rental property").

Notice is **not** required:

*   in an emergency
*   to carry out urgent repairs
*   if the property is abandoned
*   if the Tribunal so orders, or
*   if the tenant otherwise agrees.

## How to count days for a notice period

Days in the notice period are calendar days, not working days- except for smoke alarms, where the notice period is 2 business days.

All days of the week are counted, including weekends and public holidays.

The day on which the notice is served is not counted.

### Example 1

If a tenant emails or hand delivers a 21-day termination notice on 1 February, the 21 days are counted starting from 2 February.

The 21st day is 22 February. If notice is sent by post, an extra 7 working days has to be added to the notice period. Weekends, public holidays and bank holidays are not counted in the 7 days.

### Example 2

If a landlord posts a 14-day termination notice on Friday 1 February, the 7 working days for postage starts on Monday 4 February.

The notice is considered to have been served on Tuesday 12 February.

The first day of the 14-day notice period starts on Wednesday 13 and ends on Tuesday 26 February.

## List of minimum notice periods

The list below shows the reasons and the minimum notice required for entry to a property without the tenant’s consent.

These do not apply to any part of the property where the tenant does not have the right of exclusive occupation that excludes the landlord (e.g. a laundry or kitchen shared with the landlord).

### For emergencies or abandoned premises

**In an emergency**

No notice required.

**If the landlord or agent has tried and been unable to get entry with consent, and has reasonable cause for serious concern about the health and safety of the tenant or other occupants**

No notice required

**If the landlord reasonably believes the tenant has abandoned the property**

No notice required.

### For inspections and repairs

**To inspect the property**

At least 7 days' written notice each time (up to 4 times in a 12 month period)

**To carry out or assess the need for necessary repairs or maintenance**

At least 2 days notice each time.

**Urgent repairs, including fixing a burst water pipe, a gas leak or a blocked toilet.**

No notice required. Learn more about[getting urgent repairs done](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/renting-a-place-to-live/getting-repairs-done "Getting repairs done on a rental property").

**To comply with health and safety obligations**

At least 2 days notice each time.

**Health and safety obligations include inspecting swimming/spa pool fencing**

Learn more about[health and safety in a rental property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/archive-housing-and-construction-content/archived-health-safety-and-security-rental-properties "Health, safety and security in rental properties").

**To inspect or assess the need to repair or replace a smoke alarm**

At least 2 business days notice.

**To repair or replace a smoke alarm**

At least 1 hour notice.

[More information about smoke alarms](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rules/smoke-alarms-a-rental-property "Smoke alarms in a rental property").

### For property management and marketing

**To get a property valuation**

At least 7 days notice each time (once in a 12 month period).

**To take photos or videos to advertise a property for sale or rent**

Reasonable notice, and reasonable opportunity must be given for the tenant to move any belongings that can reasonably be moved out of the picture frame/video scope (only once in a 28 day period before marketing starts or the agreement ends).**Note:**A landlord or agent must not publish photos or videos of the inside of the premises which show the tenant's belongings without first obtaining the tenant's written consent.

[Learn more about privacy for tenants](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/rental-forms-surveys-and-data/resources/fair-trading-commissioners-guidance "Privacy of personal information for tenants").

**To show property to a prospective tenant**

Reasonable notice each time and only in the last 14 days before the tenancy is due to end.

**To show property to prospective buyers**

14 days’ written notice before the first inspection. After the first inspection, the tenant can agree on a suitable time frame but is not obliged to agree to more than 2 inspections per week with 48 hours notice each time.

# Rental assistant user guide

This guide explains the reviewed rental assistant interface. The guide was checked against the implemented product on 30 October 2026. Most navigation and action labels are currently Chinese; the English explanations below include those labels where helpful. Available AI assistance depends on the configured services.

This is product help. For tenancy rights, obligations and legal deadlines, use the separately cited official guidance and check its source. A property advertisement, an estimate, a saved choice and an unsigned draft each describe different stages of your search.

## Start a case and chat

Choose “New case” (New case) to start a rental workspace. Demonstration configurations may label this “New demo case”. A case holds the rental requirements, selected property, contract work and aftercare records that you save in it.

Open “AI rental assistant” (AI rental assistant). Describe your budget, whether it is per week or another period, whether it applies to a whole property, room or person, your household size, required bedrooms, bathrooms and parking, preferred areas and commute. You can start in English or Chinese. Avoid treating a monthly or per-person budget as a whole-property weekly advertisement price without checking the basis.

“New conversation” (New conversation) starts another conversation within the current case. You can return to saved conversations. A new conversation and a new case are different: use a new case when you need a separate rental workspace.

The chat can show requirement proposals, listings, comparisons, area sources and links to the relevant work screens. Review a proposed change and use its confirmation action before relying on it as saved case information. A chat response alone does not confirm a property selection or save a signed agreement.

## Edit rental requirements and see all matches

Open “My rental needs” (My rental requirements) to review or edit the current conditions. Check the budget amount, period and pricing scope; rental mode; household size; bedroom, bathroom and parking minimums; area; commute mode and maximum one-way minutes. Lifestyle preferences are also available for area reference. Confirm changes through the displayed action. If a message says the conversation or requirements have changed, reload the latest requirements before confirming.

Use the result controls to adjust a particular filter and apply the change. In “Housing recommendations” (Property recommendations), edited filter fields need “Apply filters” (Apply filters) before the displayed results reflect them. The results show their match count. All matching properties remain available through the result list, its expansion or pagination controls; the first visible cards are not the entire matching set. In chat, “View all …listings” expands a listing group; commute results have “All” (All) and area buttons plus controls to see more results.

When no property matches, review the offered changes to budget, room requirements, area or commute time. Applying a suggested relaxation changes the stated condition; read the change summary and remaining filters. You can also state the revised requirement in chat. Changing a lifestyle preference does not itself relax a hard housing or commute filter.

Open “Listing details” (Property details) for photos where available, advertised rent, room counts, commute information and a link to the original advertisement. An open-plan studio shown as a sleeping space is not proof of a separate bedroom. Verify availability, actual rent, what is included and the proposed tenancy directly with the advertiser.

## Commute estimates

Current rental discovery focuses on the University of Sydney Camperdown / Darlington main campus, with Fisher Library used as the displayed reference point. Choose a supported mode such as public transport, walking or cycling and a maximum one-way duration. Discovery uses no fixed arrival time; it does not require you to invent a class start time to compare properties.

Read the displayed approximate duration or estimated range for your selected mode. A range is a planning reference, not a guaranteed daily journey. Transport conditions and available route evidence can differ across properties. When commute information is missing, the card says that the reference is pending rather than proving the property meets your limit.

In the property details, “Google Maps” opens directions for the selected mode so you can check the journey independently. TfNSW and OpenStreetMap / FOSSGIS source references appear with the commute details. For a trip you actually intend to take, check the current route, stops and service information before travelling.

## Lifestyle preferences and sources

Tell the assistant whether parks, food and shopping, libraries or other supported lifestyle topics matter to you. “Find an area that fits your lifestyle” (Find your local area) shows relevant area context, source categories and coverage. Open the evidence details to inspect the supporting source and dates. Source categories distinguish official facility information, venue descriptions, media background and resident opinions.

Where sourced lifestyle ordering is available, it orders the properties that already meet the housing filters by coverage of your requested supported topics. Equal coverage preserves the earlier match order. It does not remove other matches, change your hard limits or establish that a property is suitable for you.

An area-level facility source does not establish distance from an individual home. Missing area coverage is not evidence that a facility is absent. Stale references, broader or neighbouring geography and background opinions do not establish a current local match. Quietness and safety are not established by these sources and do not contribute to the supported preference score. Check commute evidence separately.

## Favorites, comparison and direct selection

You have two parallel choices: select a single property directly when you are ready, or save several favorites and compare them first. Favoriting is optional; comparison is optional.

- Choose “Save listing” (Favorite property) on a card to save it. “Remove favorite” removes the favorite.
- Open “My favorites” (My favorites) to filter saved properties by address or area and open their details.
- Select 2–4 favorites to compare advertised weekly rent, bedrooms, bathrooms, parking and the displayed commute reference side by side. Chat also supports comparisons of the properties you select there.
- Choose “Select and follow up” (Select and follow up) on the property you want to carry forward. You can do this directly from a result without first favoriting or comparing it.

A favorite is not the current follow-up selection. The “Current follow-up property” label identifies the current selected property. A saved favorite that is no longer in the current catalogue may remain visible while selection is unavailable.

## Confirm selection and prepare an inspection

“Select this property and start follow-up?” (Select this property and start follow-up?) opens a confirmation dialog. Check the current property, advertised weekly rent and carried-over search conditions. Supply only the missing information requested, then choose “Confirm and start follow-up”. If another property is already selected, the dialog identifies the replacement; favorites are retained.

Confirmed selection records the property to follow up and opens the next steps. It does not book an inspection, submit a rental application or sign a tenancy. If the requirements change and the selection is marked historical, select again under the current requirements before continuing the contract workflow.

Open “Prepare inspection and enquiry” (Prepare an inspection and questions) for the “Inspection enquiry checklist” inspection question checklist. You can download the checklist and open the original advertisement. It helps you ask about:

- Whether the property is still available and when an inspection is possible.
- Actual rent, payment period and whether pricing is for the whole property, room or person.
- Included bills and other charges.
- Proposed start date, term and bond.
- Which bedrooms, bathrooms and parking spaces are included.
- Application documents, the proposed contract and landlord or agent details.

Contact the advertiser yourself and record the verified contract information in the contract screen. This checklist is a preparation aid; the screen does not provide an inspection booking or an agent-reply form. From here you can choose “Generate lease draft” (Generate lease draft) or “Review an existing contract” (Review an existing contract).

## Lease draft form, AI assistance and PDF preview

In “Contract assistant” (Contract assistant), the lease draft workflow is for the supported NSW ordinary whole-property residential tenancy form. Check that it fits the proposed arrangement before confirming. The selected property's known details can provide defaults; verify each default rather than treating it as agreed tenancy information.

Use “Enter contract details directly” (Fill contract information directly) to enter the property, landlord, agent and tenant details; proposed dates and term; rent and bond; payment information; notice addresses; occupancy and other applicable form fields. Property and each party's notice address have separate fields. Optional signing information and emergency repair contacts can be entered where the form offers them.

You can save an incomplete draft; missing items stay blank or are listed as needing confirmation. Before saving, review the confirmation summary and acknowledge that this is proposed information for an unsigned draft. “Confirm and save unsigned draft” saves a version for later review.

“AI-assisted entry (optional)” (Optional AI-assisted filling) can extract draft fields from your description when AI is configured. It asks for consent to send that text to the configured external AI. Review the proposed fields before applying them to the form. Applying AI suggestions fills the form; saving the draft still requires a separate confirmation. Direct manual entry remains available.

After saving, use “PreviewSaved… contract” to preview that saved version in the official form, or download its PDF. The preview and download show the saved version even if you have unsaved form edits. Standard terms remain in the template and signature fields remain blank. Check the completed content, missing items and attachments with the other party and arrange manual signatures. Generating a draft is not a legal-validity guarantee and does not supply the other party's agreement or signature.

## Upload a contract for review

Use “Review an existing contract” to work on a contract supplied to you. You can also upload an existing contract directly in chat or in Contract assistant without selecting a property. Record independent consent to process the uploaded document. When a current property is selected, the existing selection-bound review can additionally compare its saved information. Then choose the file, confirm you have the right to submit it and use “Upload and review” (Upload and review).

The upload control accepts TXT, DOCX and PDF up to 2,000,000 bytes. The selection-bound real-listing workflow supports text PDFs up to 30 pages; standalone and scanned PDFs support up to 10 pages. The upload control displays the applicable limit. Scanned documents depend on local OCR support.

The review first extracts fields locally. Standalone review does not infer or create a selected property. A selection-bound review additionally compares the property and recorded information. In chat, the summary shows extracted fields, findings and original evidence; the full contract page provides correction and history controls. Inspect the result and original text, including missing, uncertain or conflicting fields; correct extracted information through the available review controls after checking the source. Optional AI analysis has its own consent. Review history lets you revisit saved review versions.

“Revoke consent” (Revoke consent) withdraws permission for subsequent contract processing. This action should not be treated as deleting every previously saved case or review record. If you need private contract search as well, use its separate controls described below.

## Private contract search and separate consent

Expand “Ask more about this contract” (Ask about this contract) on the selected uploaded-contract review to search its clauses and pages. The original contract-processing permission must remain active. This contract's wording is kept separate from public product help and general NSW guidance.

- Check “I agree to create a local private search index for the current version of this contract.” and choose “Enable contract search” (Enable contract search). Rebuilding search uses the selected review version.
- The separate cloud checkbox allows the configured AI services to process the contract for embeddings and relevant excerpts for reranking and answers. Leave it unchecked for local search.
- Enter a question and use “Find contract text” (Find contract sources) for source excerpts. “Use AI for this question and relevant contract excerpts” is an additional per-question choice, available only when cloud processing is permitted.
- Use “Delete contract search index” (Forget contract search) to withdraw the contract-search permission and remove its search index. After changes to a review, reload and check the version before asking further questions.

Contract upload consent, local search consent, cloud search consent and per-question AI use are independent choices. A contract clause describes the uploaded contract's wording; it does not by itself establish the applicable law. Use the public official guidance separately when checking a legal question.

## Repair emails and follow-up records

In chat, describe the issue and requested email language and tone. The assistant shows the subject and full natural-language body before saving. Use “Copy email draft” to copy it immediately, or request a language or tone change. “Save to Aftercare” saves the exact preview after your confirmation; a missing recipient address does not block drafting. Historical previews remain copyable; rewrite controls belong to the latest assistant draft to avoid changing a different issue.

Open “Aftercare services” (Aftercare services), then “Repairs” (Day-to-day repairs). Review your saved home and contact information. Enter the landlord or agent name if known, a problem description, location, priority, email language and tone. You can prepare a draft directly or use “Polish email with AI” (AI polish email).

Clicking the polish action sends the form's original text and greeting information to the configured AI to produce an editable subject and body. Read and edit the result, then confirm saving the repair draft. If you change the original form after polishing, check the warning and regenerate or review the saved wording before continuing.

Saving or polishing does not send the email. Use “Copy email draft” (Copy email draft) or, when an email address is available, “Open in email app” (Open in email client). You review the recipient and send it yourself in your own email application. Without an address you can still save and copy the draft.

Update the saved repair status and use “Record repair follow-up” (Record repair follow-up) to record a reply or your own notes. “Adjust email tone” changes draft wording for the existing repair. These actions update the repair record without contacting the recipient. For an urgent problem, use the saved emergency contact and the official guidance shown in the interface rather than relying on a draft as an emergency response.

## Utilities, moving and cleaning providers

In “Utilities” (Utilities), open provider cards to view the provider's coverage, contact details, official website, source and checked date. Where available, details include plan or tariff information and its source. Confirm current availability, price and conditions for your actual address with the provider.

Select electricity, gas, internet and the applicable water provider in the form, then use “Save provider selection” (Save provider choices) and confirm. This stores your choices in the workspace; it does not open or switch an account. The water information is shown for the provider serving the address rather than as an unrestricted switching choice.

In “Moving and cleaning” (Moving and cleaning), click a company card to open its details and official website. “Record quote or booking” (Record a quote or booking) lets you save a quote you received, a service date, status and notes. Status choices distinguish considering, contacted by you, booked by you and completed.

Saving a service record does not submit a booking. Contact the company and arrange the work yourself; provider availability, service coverage and the quote need the company's confirmation. Return to “My service records” to update the record after your own arrangements.

## Move-out plans and bond follow-up

The aftercare workspace also provides “Move-out plan” (Move-out plan) and “Bond follow-up” (Bond follow-up). Review the tenancy information and any source-based prefill before saving it. Missing home information can be completed through the provided form. You can register supporting evidence and attach its references to the appropriate tasks or facts.

For a move-out plan, choose the intended date and confirm the practical schedule. Tasks can record progress, supporting evidence and items needing human review. A date change is proposed and then explicitly confirmed; completed work and evidence remain part of the history. Plan dates are practical arrangements, not statements of legal notice deadlines. Reminders depend on the workspace settings and do not contact service providers for you.

For bond follow-up, establish the record and supply a bond reference or linked deposit evidence before activating follow-up. Record the facts you report, their dates in Sydney time, supporting evidence and any deduction claims made by the other party. Recording a deduction claim does not mean you accept it. Disputed claims or conflicting evidence can require human review before a follow-up draft can be generated.

“Prepare factual draft” (Prepare factual draft) creates wording from the saved facts; optional AI assistance can help select supported points when enabled and consented to. Review and copy the draft for your own use. Drafts are not automatically sent and the workspace does not submit a bond refund or dispute application. You can record further facts, confirm the actual outcome or withdraw follow-up. Check official sources separately for the applicable process and deadlines.

## Read sources and handle changes

“Ask rental knowledge” searches public knowledge separately from private contract search. “Find sources” can show relevant source excerpts without choosing the optional AI consent. If you allow the question and relevant public excerpts to be sent to the configured AI services, read the returned citations and any stated uncertainty. Public product documentation explains controls; official guidance supplies tenancy information.

Saved data and current form input can differ. If you see a stale-version warning or a failed-save message, use the offered reload or retry action, compare the latest information with your retained input and confirm again. A visible proposed value or an unsaved preview is not proof that a write completed. “Case progress” (Case progress) helps you revisit the recorded stages.
